Spirits

It was a gradual process. One after the other, the skyscrapers grew by themselves: concrete sprouted from concrete, rebar burrowed into the ground, buildings would shed their fiberglass in fall and then regrow it come spring. In summer, when the sun beats down on their walls, you can feel them sucking up its energy and contracting as it pulses through them. It’s not dilation; you can sense that they’re full of life. The walls twitch when you hammer in a nail. Towns became cities, cities became megacities… New York at present covers up most of the East Coast, Shanghai stretches thousands of miles inland—yet there are few people left to inhabit them. The population is spread out so thin that you could walk for hours without meeting another human being; all you could see would be boulevards and avenues, parks and playgrounds, parking lots and skyscrapers, stretching (seemingly) into infinity.

When you do meet someone on the street, they usually aren’t human. The spirits started coming in limited numbers at first, but now they’re almost everywhere. They’re mostly silent and keep to themselves. If you engage them in conversation, they’ll bore you until you leave. I had not thought death had undone so many… In fact, I have the distinct feeling that many of them aren’t even wearing faces of the dead, that theirs are mere extrapolations of faces that had once existed, an endless procession of imitations.

Then there’s the water. Slowly it became clearer and clearer and clearer still, until it was like glass, like crystal—you could look down into the ocean and see hundreds of meters below, all the fish suspended as if in resin, except they kept moving about. And water continued to get clearer and clearer every day until you couldn’t even see it anymore. You could walk in and swim in it, of course, take a sip and taste the salt and refuse, but from the outside it seemed like you were swimming in nothing and drinking air. One of my friends who used to be a fisherman by trade had to move away, because the concrete jungle didn’t seem all that scary compared to what he had seen back at the shore. He told me about it often, he couldn’t get it out of his mind. He said it didn’t worry him at first, that he had got used to it—it all happened so gradually after all—but then he visited his mother inland, not a lake or river in sight, and when he came back (after maybe a week without seeing large bodies of water?), the sight of the ocean knocked him out cold: a fishing boat rocking above a crevasse some hundred meters high, as if floating around on air; a manta ray flapping its wings about, suspended on some inexistent thread; a long-forgotten shipwreck on the bottom, so far down he could only make out the general shape… He had to go on a fishing boat that same afternoon (you still had to work then) and he wanted to call it off, to stay on shore, but he couldn’t. It took a while before he found the courage to step onto the seemingly unstable vessel, but he managed, he sleepwaltzed onto it and sat down, his entire body trembling. His comrades kidded him, said he’d pass out as soon as they raised the anchor, but he sat unspeaking and closed his eyes. The sun kissed his face, the gentle wind caressed him, it was all as it had ever been, except for the sound: the unseen waves rocked the boat back and forth without a single splash, the deep rumble he had grown used to was entirely absent. They set off and my friend, terrified as he was, fainted. His comrades left him on the floor and only revived him when they returned.

As is, I think, apparent, not all fishermen found the new water intolerable. I’m friends with another one who told me that it’s just a matter of getting used to it: “The water’s still there, even if you can’t see it. You just have to pretend like you can, and you’ll have no trouble swimming and diving in it.” Matter of fact, he is actually quite fond of being able to see for miles into the depths. He said it gives you perspective, lets you see your life in a larger context. I wouldn’t know. I hate swimming.

You know all that, of course. I tell it to you every day it seems, but I still don’t know what to think of it. I think the word used to be “strange.” Yes, it’s strange. It all has to have a meaning, has to serve a purpose or have a cause. What would the purpose be? A punishment—or maybe a reward? This is how you imagine punishment? Silent, invisible seas, skyscrapers that grow like trees, the dead com’g back to life? Shouldn’t the sea turn red? It did, back in the ancient times, and it wasn’t a punishment but an omen. What would it be if not a punishment? And anyway, I don’t think they’re the spirits of the dead… Your problem is that you look for a cause behind everything. You’re no better than the mediævals. Are you go’g to start whip’g yourself? Not that, what I mean is, there is no event that has no cause, except one. Who’s to say this isn’t a second? You mean: a period of transition, the time of monsters. Two causae primae overlaid, two worlds colliding. I’m not say’g anything, I just want you to realise how misguide’d your search for a “cause” and a “reason” is. Might as well ask what’s the purpose of a tree. The tree might not have a purpose, but it does have a cause. Science began by investigating the causes of what is. And it’s how it end’d when the concrete started grow’g and water grew invisible. What about the fish y’r friend saw? Do they care about why the water was clear? No—they keep swim’g and flap’g their fins. “Tiere… sie schöpfen die Kraft, Kinder zu gebären, ja, zu essen, aus dem Gefühl der Stetigkeit, der Notwendigkeit…”[1] they know it’s necessary and that it has a continuity of sorts, and that’s enough. Why do you need more than that? Fish are one thing, and good on them—“eppur si muove!”[2] What concern is it of yours? Eppur the skyscrapers grow, eppur you see shipwrecks at the bottom of the ocean, eppur spirits visit us… I’d like to believe that the spirits of yore were a little more dignified. I wonder how happy Hamlet would be to listen to the spirit of his father had it been like one of ours. You can barely understand them! Their words twist in agony at having to exist in two places simultaneously. Oh, come off it. They don’t know what they’re saying, they’re just putting words in roughly the right order and praying for the best. If you tell them they aren’t real people, they just laugh at you—oh God, those hollow laughs of theirs… What if you are one of them? Very original. Anyway, it’s almost half past six. Same time tomorrow?

Her departures were always unproblematic. I suppose it’s easier when you share memories and don’t have the notion of self. She always leaves thinking she’ll come back the day after, even though she might not—I don’t even know if she kept on existing after I closed the door behind her. She might remember today, or not. She might remember most of it and exaggerate some events, or make up something she or I had said as well as the answer to it. In a way, I envy her. I might share her fate one day.

  1. “Animals… they draw the strength to bear children, even to eat, from a sense of continuity, of necessity.” ↩︎

  2. “And yet it moves!” ↩︎
